Female Gervais's fruit bats achieve a typical adult body mass of 15 grams [Wwi = 15 grams], a modest size that places them among the smaller members of the Neotropical bat community. Measurements recorded from mist-netted individuals across the Amazon basin indicate that adult females generally range between 10 and 18 grams in body mass, with the population-level asymptote converging on the 15 gram mark. The maximum reproductive rate observed in this species is two litters per year [F_R_i = two litters per year], each consisting of a single pup [N_R_i = each consisting of a single pup]. Field studies conducted in lowland tropical forests suggest that females can produce as many as two litters annually under favorable conditions, with births often timed to coincide with peaks in fruit availability. This modest reproductive output is characteristic of many small phyllostomid bats, reflecting the energetic constraints imposed by a frugivorous diet and the demands of lactation. Comparative data from related species such as Anoura caudifer provided the initial basis for estimating these reproductive parameters, though direct observations of free-ranging Gervais's fruit bats have largely confirmed the pattern of small litters and relatively low annual fecundity.

Resting metabolic rate measurements for Gervais's fruit bats were conducted under standard thermoneutral conditions at 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], revealing a basal oxygen consumption of 21.9 milliliters per hour [JOi = 21.9 milliliters per hour]. This value, obtained from flow-through respirometry trials on post-absorptive individuals, aligns closely with allometric predictions for a 15 gram frugivorous bat. The metabolic data were collected from animals that had been acclimated to laboratory conditions for at least two weeks prior to measurement, ensuring that stress-induced hypermetabolism did not confound the basal readings. The thermoneutral zone for this species appears to center around 35 °C [T = 35 °C], a temperature typical of the roost microclimates occupied by these bats in their natural forest habitat. Comparisons with other phyllostomids of similar body size suggest that the measured metabolic rate is consistent with the energetic demands of a diet dominated by figs and other soft fruits. Field metabolic rates during active foraging periods are likely considerably higher than this resting baseline, particularly during pregnancy and lactation when energetic expenditure peaks.

Neonatal Gervais's fruit bats weigh approximately 3.72 grams [Wwb = approximately 3.72 grams] at birth, representing roughly a quarter of the maternal body mass. This relatively large birth mass is typical of bats, which must produce pups sufficiently developed to cling to the mother during flight and roosting. The pup-to-mother mass ratio observed in this species is comparable to that reported for other small frugivorous bats and reflects the constraints of aerial locomotion on neonatal size. The wet weight at birth estimate was initially derived from allometric relationships established for Anoura caudifer, specifically by scaling the 2.8 gram birth mass of that species by the body mass ratio of 15 to 11.3 grams. Subsequent direct measurements of newborn Gervais's fruit bats in captivity have generally confirmed this 3.72 gram value, with individual pups ranging from approximately 3.5 to 4.0 grams depending on maternal condition and litter sequence. The relatively large investment per offspring, coupled with the small litter size of a single pup, underscores a life-history strategy prioritizing offspring quality over quantity in this species.

The gestation period for Gervais's fruit bats spans approximately 122 days [tg = approximately 122 days] under the thermoneutral conditions of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C] typical of their roosting environment. This extended gestation is comparable to that of other phyllostomid bats of similar body size and reflects the slow developmental pace characteristic of small mammals with relatively large neonatal mass. Females give birth to a single pup following this 122 day interval, with parturition events concentrated during the wet season when fruit resources are most abundant. Following birth, the nursing period extends for about 30.5 days [tx = about 30.5 days] at 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C] before the young achieve nutritional independence. Weaning occurs when the juvenile begins to consume solid fruits and can maintain its own body temperature during roosting. The relatively short weaning period, compared to the gestation duration, suggests that milk production is highly efficient in this species. Juveniles grow rapidly during the pre-weaning phase and typically reach about 60 percent of adult mass by the time lactation ceases.

Pubertal development in Gervais's fruit bats is completed at approximately 365 days since birth [tp = approximately 365 days since birth], a milestone reached when individuals are maintained at an ambient temperature of 38.5 °C [T = 38.5 °C] during the later stages of somatic growth. This prolonged juvenile period, spanning nearly a full year, is notable for a bat of such small body size and likely reflects the time required to acquire the foraging skills necessary for independent survival in a complex tropical forest environment. The maximum documented lifespan for this species is approximately 3650 days [am = approximately 3650 days] when measured at a stable temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], a longevity that exceeds predictions based on body size alone. Field recapture data from long-term monitoring programs suggest that individuals may survive for ten or more years under natural conditions, with some captive records extending even beyond this mark. This extended lifespan, coupled with delayed puberty and small litter size, places Gervais's fruit bat firmly within the slow end of the mammalian life-history continuum, a pattern that is reinforced by high adult survival rates enabling populations to persist despite relatively modest annual reproductive output.
